Because Divine Unity and Justice are the two principles in which the rational method and philosophical outlook of the major Muʿtazilite thinkers appear most clearly, we will limit our study of Muʿtazilite doctrine to these two principles, taking each of them in a separate chapter.
1 — What the Muʿtazilites Meant by Divine Unity

The principle of divine unity, in its broadest sense, is shared by all Muslims. All Muslims also regard it as one of the basic foundations of Islam. But the Muʿtazilites developed their own distinctive interpretation of it.

In doing so, they entered directly into the language of philosophy and used logical categories of the kind normally found in metaphysical discussion. What is especially striking is that they began with a philosophical position rather than with the Islamic texts dealing with the subject.

In other words, they first established the theoretical principle through reason and logical categories. Only then did they return to the religious texts. They accepted those that agreed with what they had already established rationally, and they reinterpreted texts whose apparent meaning seemed to conflict with their theory.
For them, then, reason was the first authority. Revelation had to be interpreted in a way that agreed with reason.
This is what ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd, one of the leading early Muʿtazilite teachers, meant when he said:
“Religion is the establishment of God’s proof in the minds of those who are morally responsible.”
On this basis, the Muʿtazilite discussion of divine unity begins as follows.

God is one. But they did not mean this in the simple sense accepted by Muslim traditionalists. They meant that God’s essence is simple, in the philosophical sense of the word: it is not made up of parts.
The divine essence cannot be composite.
The reason is that anything composite necessarily involves two things.

First, a whole cannot exist unless every one of its parts exists. The whole therefore depends on each of its parts. If God’s essence were made up of parts, God would depend on those parts for his existence. But this is impossible, because dependence implies weakness and inability.
Second, composition requires multiplicity, and multiplicity contradicts unity.

If something is made up of parts, each part must be different from every other part, and each part must also be different from the whole. We therefore end up with several distinct things: each part is one thing, while the whole itself is another thing.
There is also the problem of dependence again. Each of these distinct things depends for its existence on the others.

So, by following the logical implications of the category of whole and part, the Muʿtazilites denied that God’s essence could be composite. They therefore affirmed its simplicity, which they saw as the core meaning of divine unity.
To say that “God is one,” then, means that there is absolutely no multiplicity in his essence, either in quantity or in essence.

The result is that every feature belonging to natural or human bodies must be denied of God. This includes personal and bodily features, as well as color, smell, dimensions, directions, and anything else that would imply bodily existence and therefore composition.

We can reconstruct this rational interpretation of divine unity from several sources. Some were written by Muʿtazilite thinkers themselves, while most were preserved by historians of Islamic sects such as al-Shahrastānī, al-Masʿūdī, Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī, Aḥmad ibn Yaḥyā al-Murtaḍā, and others.
Among the Muʿtazilite texts is this statement by al-Qāḍī ʿAbd al-Jabbār:

“The Muʿtazilites unanimously agree that the world has an eternal creator who is powerful, knowing, and living, but not through separate meanings”—that is, these attributes are not meanings distinct from God’s essence—“and that he is not a body, an accident, or a substance, but one single being who cannot be perceived by any sense.”

“Their doctrine concerning the first principle, the principle of divine unity, is what all the Muʿtazilites of Basra, Baghdad, and elsewhere agreed upon, despite their differences on other secondary questions: that God, mighty and exalted, is unlike all things; that he is neither body, accident, element, part, nor substance, but rather the creator of bodies, accidents, elements, parts, and substances; that none of the senses can perceive him in this world or the next; that no place contains him and no dimension surrounds him; that he has always existed, with no time, place, end, or limit; that he created all things and brought them into existence from nothing; and that he alone is eternal, while everything else came into existence.”
Al-Shahrastānī also lists among the points on which the Muʿtazilites agreed:

“The complete denial that God resembles material beings in any respect: in direction, place, form, body, occupation of space, movement, disappearance, change, or being affected. They therefore required figurative interpretation of the ambiguous texts that appear to suggest such things.”

There is also a much fuller text explaining what divine unity meant to the Muʿtazilites. It is worth quoting in full because we will need many parts of it later when we examine different sides of the Muʿtazilite concept of divine unity.
Al-Ashʿarī preserves the following account of their position:

“God is one. Nothing is like him. He is the Hearing and the Seeing. He is not a body, shape, mass, image, flesh, blood, person, substance, or accident. He has no color, taste, smell, or texture. He is neither hot nor cold, wet nor dry. He has no length, width, or depth. He is not joined or separated. He neither moves nor remains still. He cannot be divided and has no divisions, parts, limbs, or organs. He has no direction: no right or left, front or back, above or below. No place surrounds him and no time passes over him. He cannot touch or be separated from things, nor can he dwell in places. He cannot be described by any of the qualities of created beings that show that they came into existence—that is, that they are created rather than eternal. He cannot be described as having a measurable limit or as extending in any direction. He is not bounded, nor does he beget or have a parent. Measures do not contain him, veils do not conceal him, the senses do not perceive him, and he cannot be measured by comparison with human beings.

“He does not resemble creation in any respect. No affliction or defect can touch him. Whatever occurs to the mind or can be imagined does not resemble him. He has always existed first, before all things that came into being, and existed before all created things. He has always been knowing, powerful, and living, and he will always remain so.

“Eyes do not see him, sight does not grasp him, imagination does not encompass him, and ears do not hear him. He is a thing unlike other things: knowing, powerful, and living, but unlike those among created beings who know, have power, and live.

“He alone is eternal. Nothing else is eternal. There is no god but him. He has no partner in his kingdom, no minister in his rule”—that is, no supporter or helper—“and no assistant in bringing into being what he creates. He did not create the world from a previous model. Creating one thing is no easier for him than creating another, nor is anything more difficult for him.

“He cannot seek benefits for himself, nor can harm reach him. He does not experience pleasure or delight, and injury and pain cannot touch him. He has no final limit at which he would come to an end. He cannot perish, nor can weakness or deficiency affect him.”
2 — Between the Traditionalists and the Muʿtazilites
If we take this account preserved by al-Ashʿarī together with the other reports on the Muʿtazilite idea of divine unity, we can draw the following general picture.
When the Muʿtazilites say that God is “one,” they do not mean numerical oneness in the simple everyday sense of the word.
They mean that, as the Qurʾān says, “there is nothing like him.”
But this Qurʾānic statement gives only the general principle. The Muʿtazilites believed that reason must analyze it using clear philosophical concepts.
This was different from the approach taken by the people of the Sunna and the Community, the Sunni traditionalists.

The traditionalists accepted the verse “There is nothing like him” through faith, without trying to analyze its philosophical implications. At the same time, they also accepted other Qurʾānic verses and prophetic traditions whose apparent wording seems to conflict with it by describing God in terms that resemble living, bodily beings.
They accepted these texts as they stood, again as a matter of faith, without trying to explain the apparent contradiction or interpret the language figuratively.

Their reasoning was that the Qurʾān is God’s word and must therefore be believed exactly as God revealed it. Any attempt to reinterpret the text would replace the meaning given by God with a meaning reached by the human interpreter.
There was another problem as well. Interpretation is a human act and can therefore be mistaken. Different people can also reach different interpretations depending on their views and positions.
The Muʿtazilites rejected this approach in two ways.
First, they used reason to examine the very idea of a God who created the universe.
Second, they also used reason to examine the Islamic religious texts that describe this God.

On the first point, they argued that reason itself requires us to deny anything that would imply composition in God’s essence. We must therefore also deny everything that bodily existence would require: parts, organs, dimensions, directions, place, time, substance, and accident.
All of these things conflict with the unity that must belong to the creator of the universe.
Divine unity, understood in this sense as freedom from bodily form, is therefore necessary for an eternal creator.
Once reason has established this, they argued, we must accept the clear Qurʾānic verses that agree with reason, such as:
Other verses whose apparent wording suggests bodily qualities must then be interpreted in a way that brings them into agreement with reason.
“The hand of God is over their hands.” Qurʾān 48:10
Taken literally, this appears to give God a “hand.”
“And the face of your Lord will remain.” Qurʾān 55:27
Taken literally, this appears to give God a “face.”
Taken literally, this appears to give God “eyes.”
“The Most Merciful established himself upon the Throne.” Qurʾān 20:5
Taken literally, this appears to describe physical sitting on a physical object, the Throne understood as a seat.
“Do you feel secure from the One who is in heaven?” Qurʾān 67:16
Taken literally, this appears to assign God a place.
“They fear their Lord above them.” Qurʾān 16:50
Taken literally, this appears to assign God a direction: above them.
The Muʿtazilites therefore interpreted these verses rationally in ways that removed their apparent physical meaning.

Words with a direct physical meaning were taken figuratively or symbolically. “Hand,” for example, was understood as power. God’s being established on the Throne was understood as majesty and exaltedness. “Eyes” referred to care and intention, and so on.
This, then, is the Muʿtazilite idea of divine unity.
As we can see, it is philosophical in character and rests on philosophical categories such as whole and part, place and time, directions and dimensions, and substance and accident.
This special interpretation of divine unity led the Muʿtazilites to adopt a number of rational positions that also differed from those of the traditionalists.
The nature of our study requires us to examine each of these questions carefully.
A — The Question of God’s Attributes
This was one of the earliest questions to become extremely important in Muʿtazilite thought.
Adam Mez goes so far as to say:

“Because the Muʿtazilites made discussion of God’s essence and attributes the main subject of their theology, this question not only became one of the most important questions of Islamic doctrine down to the present day; their discussion of it also gave Arab philosophy a distinctive character.”
This is an exaggeration, but it points us toward an important question: how did the problem begin?
The Qurʾān describes God with attributes such as knowing, powerful, living, hearing, seeing, and speaking.

The Muslim traditionalists held that these attributes were eternal just as God was eternal. They were inseparable from his essence, and since his essence was eternal, his attributes must also be eternal.
Then Jahm ibn Ṣafwān, leader of the Jabrites, introduced a new position. In opposition to the traditionalists who came before him, he denied that God possessed attributes in this sense.

Jahm’s reason was that assigning such attributes to God would make God resemble some of his creatures, especially human beings. Human beings too are described as hearing, seeing, living, speaking, and so on.
When the Muʿtazilites appeared, they also denied God’s attributes in the sense already proposed by Jahm. But they based their argument on their own concept of divine unity.
For them, the denial of separate attributes followed necessarily from that concept.
Reason had already established, in their view, that God’s unity means that his essence is simple and cannot be composite in the philosophical sense of simple and composite.
They were therefore forced to deny the existence of any eternal attribute that existed in addition to God’s essence or separately from it.
If an attribute were something additional to or different from the divine essence, there would be more than one eternal reality. That would amount to a plurality of gods.
This first explanation of the problem appeared with Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ, the founder of the Muʿtazilite school. Later thinkers developed it into much more philosophically complex forms.
Al-Shahrastānī noticed this development from simpler to more complex explanations.

“was immature at first. Wāṣil ibn ʿAṭāʾ began with an obvious”—that is, not very deep—“argument: there was general agreement that two eternal gods cannot exist. Wāṣil therefore said: anyone who affirms an eternal meaning and an eternal attribute has affirmed two gods.”
This was how the question was first explained in Wāṣil’s time.
As al-Shahrastānī rightly observes, it was still an elementary argument. It lacked the more developed philosophical analysis that later thinkers would bring to the problem.
